title: A Inventory for the Aftermath
premise: Yara Kavanagh, a piano tuner who reads a building's past in its pipes and radiators, has spent thirty years drifting between other people's houses, keeping his own history locked in a childhood home he never visits. When that house—the one where his sister died and his family quietly arranged itself around her absence—goes up for auction, he returns to tune the piano one last time and finds his estranged brother, Declan, already there, buying back the past with money Yara never knew he had. As the auction deadline closes in, Yara must finally ask the question the whole family built its silence around: who was really to blame the night Nell died. The novel ends with Yara refusing both brothers' bargains and instead opening the house as a free music school for the neighborhood, choosing found family over inherited guilt.
about_author: Juniper Almeida is the pen name of a former building restorer who spent a decade crawling through the basements and boiler rooms of old houses, collecting their sounds. They write from a converted schoolhouse in coastal Maine, where the radiators still knock out their opinions every morning.

chapters.title: The Tuner's Ear
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. We meet him mid-job, tuning a grand piano in a stranger's parlor while narrating the house's emotional history through its radiators—a widow's grief, a divorce in the walls. He is precise, invisible, unattached. The beat is quiet loneliness dressed as professional pride.

chapters.title: Tenant of My Own Life
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. His rented room, his ritual of never signing leases longer than a year, his careful avoidance of his hometown, Kilternan. A letter arrives: the Kavanagh house is entering probate auction. His hands shake on the tuning lever for the first time in years. Beat: dread disguised as irritation.

chapters.title: What the Radiators Remember
chapters.summary: Yara's POV, flashback braided in. Driving back toward Kilternan, he recalls learning to 'hear' houses as a boy with Nell, who claimed the boiler spoke in their mother's voice. He arrives to find the house already occupied—by Declan, who has made an offer before auction. Beat: the past ambushing the present.

chapters.title: Declan's Ledger
chapters.summary: Declan's POV. Declan, prosperous and controlled, sees the house as a debt to be settled and an image to be managed. He offers Yara money to sign away his share and stay away. We see his tenderness curdle into control. Beat: love expressed as purchase.

chapters.title: The Piano in the Front Room
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Inside the shuttered house, he finds Nell's upright piano, untouched, and begins tuning it against Declan's orders. Each note unlocks a memory: Nell at eleven, Nell the summer before she died. Beat: grief as a physical, audible thing.

chapters.title: The Question Nobody Asked
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. He reconstructs the night Nell drowned in the cistern—who was meant to be watching, who lied at the inquest. The family's silence arranged itself around an unspoken verdict. Beat: the mystery sharpens from atmosphere to accusation.

chapters.title: Maeve at the Gate
chapters.summary: Maeve's POV. Their aunt Maeve, the house's reluctant keeper, arrives with a casserole and a warning: let the auction happen, let the past stay buried. But her hands betray her—she has kept Nell's room locked for thirty years. Beat: complicity wearing the mask of kindness.

chapters.title: Auction Notices
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. The auction is publicized; strangers tramp through the house appraising it, and Yara hears them misreading it completely. A teenage girl, Saoirse, sneaks in to play the untuned piano, and Yara hears in her something of Nell. Beat: the house becoming a contested object rather than a home.

chapters.title: Declan's Offer, Revised
chapters.summary: Declan's POV. Under pressure from his own family to sell the house for development, Declan raises his offer to Yara and asks for something stranger: Yara's public silence about the past at the auction. Beat: the corruption of power—Declan buying not property but narrative.

chapters.title: The Cistern
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Yara descends into the drained cistern and finds evidence he was too young to understand at eight: a rusted latch that was broken before that night. Someone could have gotten in—or out. Beat: the ground shifting under thirty years of assumed guilt.

chapters.title: What Maeve Kept
chapters.summary: Maeve's POV. Maeve finally opens Nell's room: letters, a broken music box, and a confession never sent. She was the one meant to watch the children that evening; she left to take a phone call from a married man. Beat: the weight of a secret kept out of shame rather than malice.

chapters.title: Brother Against the Boiler
chapters.summary: Yara and Declan, alternating close third. A confrontation in the basement: Yara accuses Declan of knowing about the latch, of letting the family believe a child wandered off. Declan admits he saw Maeve leave and said nothing—to punish her, and his parents, for a lifetime of small cruelties. Beat: the family's architecture of blame exposed as a choice, not a fate.

chapters.title: Saoirse's Recital
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Saoirse returns to practice on the piano; Yara teaches her, and the house fills with sound for the first time in decades. Neighbors gather on the lawn, uninvited, listening. Beat: found family beginning to assemble itself around music rather than silence.

chapters.title: The Developer's Men
chapters.summary: Declan's POV. The development consortium pressures Declan, threatening his business; his offer to Yara becomes a threat—sign, or the house goes to demolition anyway. Declan realizes he has become the thing he hated. Beat: power completing its corruption.

chapters.title: Maeve's Letter, Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Yara reads Maeve's unsent confession aloud in the kitchen with Declan and Maeve present. The room's radiators, in his hearing, finally go quiet. Maeve asks neither forgiveness nor punishment—only to be heard. Beat: catharsis without absolution.

chapters.title: Auction Day
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converging. The auction on the front lawn: Declan bidding against developers, Yara holding his signed-away share like a stone, Saoirse's family watching. At the final call, Yara stands and asks the question aloud—the question the family arranged itself around—in front of everyone. Beat: the climax, public and irreversible.

chapters.title: What Declan Bought
chapters.summary: Declan's POV. Declan wins the auction, outbidding the developers, and stands in the emptied house realizing he purchased a mausoleum. Yara refuses his final check. Beat: hollow victory, the emptiness of ownership without reckoning.

chapters.title: The Counteroffer
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Yara proposes the impossible: Declan keeps the deed, but the house becomes a free music school, with Maeve as caretaker and Yara as tuner-in-residence. Declan, stripped of every other use for the house, must decide what he actually wanted. Beat: love offered one last time, on new terms.

chapters.title: Signing
chapters.summary: Declan's POV. Declan signs the agreement in the same kitchen where the family's silence was manufactured. Maeve brings tea; no one apologizes in words, but everyone stays past the point where they could have left. Beat: reconciliation as practice, not feeling.

chapters.title: First Lesson
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. The first students arrive—Saoirse and a dozen neighborhood kids. Yara tunes the upright and hears, for the first time, not the house's grief but its patience. Beat: the found family taking shape in real time.

chapters.title: Nell's Room, Open
chapters.summary: Yara and Maeve's shared chapter. They clear Nell's room together and turn it into a practice room, keeping only the broken music box on the sill. Yara finally says Nell's name aloud without flinching. Beat: mourning completed, not erased.

chapters.title: An Inventory for the Aftermath
chapters.summary: Yara's POV, final. A year later, Yara signs his first long lease—his own name on the caretaker's flat. He walks the house cataloguing what remains: pianos, radiators, people. The novel ends with him teaching Saoirse to listen to a house, passing on the inheritance that was never written down. Beat: belonging, at last, chosen rather than inherited.
